title: Chennai NGO REACH Wins Kochon Prize 2026, a First for an Indian NGO
excerpt: The tuberculosis-care organisation, founded in 1999 to link Chennai's private doctors with the public TB programme, receives the Stop TB Partnership's global honour.
body:
• REACH, a Chennai-based non-governmental organisation working on tuberculosis care since 1999, has received the Kochon Prize 2026, The Hindu reported.
  • REACH is the first Indian NGO to win the prize; earlier Indian recipients were a government TB programme head in 2006, the Indian Council of Medical Research in 2017 and a diagnostics company in 2025.
  • The Kochon Prize, awarded through the Stop TB Partnership and funded by South Korea's Kochon Foundation, carries a medal and US$65,000 and honours significant contributions to the fight against TB.
  • REACH's model links India's public TB programme with private practitioners in Chennai — including more than 40 Nakshatra Centre hubs — and trains people affected by TB as community advocates.

REACH, a Chennai-based non-governmental organisation that has worked on tuberculosis care for more than 25 years, has received the Kochon Prize 2026 for advancing TB care, The Hindu reported. The award makes REACH the first Indian NGO to win the prize, according to Rising Kashmir's report of the announcement.

What the prize is

The Kochon Prize is awarded each year through the Stop TB Partnership to individuals or organisations that have made a significant contribution to combating tuberculosis. Funded by the Kochon Foundation of South Korea, it consists of a medal and US$65,000, and it is among the longest-running international honours in TB work. India has won it before, but never through an NGO: the 2006 recipient was Dr L. S. Chauhan, then head of the Indian government's TB programme; the Indian Council of Medical Research won in 2017; and in 2025 the prize went to Molbio Diagnostics, the first private company to receive it, for its Truenat molecular testing platform. REACH's win puts a community-based non-profit alongside those government and industry recipients.

What REACH does

REACH — the Resource Group for Education and Advocacy for Community Health — was established in Chennai in 1999, as the Revised National TB Control Programme was rolling out in Tamil Nadu, and is led by its director, Dr Nalini Krishnan. Its mandate covers support, care and treatment for TB patients as well as research, advocacy and public education, and it works in partnership with what is now the National TB Elimination Programme at national, state and district levels.

The organisation's signature model is an interface between the public system and private healthcare, where most Indians first seek care. Through its private-sector engagement strategy, REACH supports private practitioners to identify, diagnose and treat people with TB, operating more than 40 private-provider hubs called Nakshatra Centres across Chennai — a model that has become an integral part of the Greater Chennai Corporation's TB Free Chennai initiative, according to REACH's own programme description. REACH also helped build a network of TB Champions — people affected by TB who advocate in their own communities — and since 2018 has worked on non-communicable diseases alongside its TB programmes.

Why it matters

India carries the world's largest TB burden, and the gap the prize recognises is the one REACH was built to close: patients who start treatment in the private sector and risk falling outside the public programme's notification, drug-supply and follow-up systems. A global prize for that bridging work is a marker that community-level linkage — not only new drugs and diagnostics — is part of how India expects to meet its TB elimination goals. For REACH, the recognition arrives in its 27th year of work, still headquartered in Chennai and still working the same seam between the clinic, the programme and the patient.
